items.title: State models + persistence layer
items.description: Pydantic models implementing the versioned state schema from spec.md (schema_version, run_id, ticket_id, status, phase, write_scope, reviewer_rejection_history, retry_bound, budget, interrupt_log). Local JSON load/save matching regiment-backlog.json conventions.
acceptance_criteria: Pydantic models validate all fields listed in spec.md's state schema draft
State can be saved to and loaded from a local JSON file
A second CLI invocation can resume from a prior run's saved state file
Invalid/malformed state on load raises a clear validation error, not a silent pass
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 1
items.notes: Nothing else in the backlog can be built without this landing first.

items.title: Per-node write-scope tool binding
items.description: Tool-binding factory (ADR-002) that constructs each node's LangGraph tool set at graph-build time, scoped only to that node's declared write paths.
acceptance_criteria: A node's tool set contains no write tool capable of touching a path outside its declared scope
Attempting an out-of-scope write fails structurally (missing tool), not via a runtime permission check
Test exists per node confirming its exact tool set matches its declared scope
items.source: docs/adrs/adr0002.md; plan.md sequencing step 2
items.notes: Interrupt trigger #2 becomes defense-in-depth once this lands, per ADR-002 — still log attempted out-of-scope calls.

items.title: LiteLLM client wrapper
items.description: Per-node model configuration wrapper over LiteLLM, allowing each node to specify its own model/provider independently.
acceptance_criteria: Each node can be configured with a different model via LiteLLM without code changes to the node itself
A failed LiteLLM call after configured retries surfaces as a distinct infra-failure state, not an unhandled exception
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 3
items.notes: Retry-then-fail behavior here feeds directly into interrupt trigger #5 (BTN-8).

items.title: Architect node
items.description: Native LangGraph node rewrite of Architect: produces plan.md-equivalent output and backlog ticket(s) from spec-level input, scoped to its declared write paths.
acceptance_criteria: Given a spec-equivalent input, produces plan output matching the state schema's expected shape
Cannot write outside its declared scope (verified via BTN-2's test pattern)
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 4

items.title: Driver node
items.description: Native LangGraph node rewrite of Driver: implements a ticket in a red-green-refactor cycle, scoped to its declared write paths.
acceptance_criteria: Given an Architect-produced ticket, produces implementation output matching expected state shape
Cannot write outside its declared scope
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 5
items.notes: Built against Architect's output shape once BTN-4 lands. SCOPE NOTE: implements scoped multi-file output from a single LLM call, per this ticket's literal AC. Does not execute the tests it writes to verify real red-then-green — that would require sandboxed pytest execution across multiple LLM calls, a materially bigger capability. Flagged before implementation; deferred, not silently assumed covered.

items.title: Reviewer node
items.description: Native LangGraph node rewrite of Reviewer: skeptical review of Driver's output, with consistent root-cause articulation on rejection to support interrupt trigger #1. Verification is re-run from a clean tree independent of Driver's working state, not taken on Driver's self-report.
acceptance_criteria: Given Driver output, produces an accept/reject verdict with a stated root cause on rejection
Root cause is expressed consistently enough across cycles to support same-cause-twice detection
Tests/checks are re-run from a clean checkout, not read from Driver's self-reported pass/fail
Cannot write outside its declared scope
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 6; plan.md Risks section; github.com/Sdraugel/albert clean-tree verification pattern
items.notes: Prompt design for consistent root-cause articulation needs explicit attention, not just plumbing — flagged in plan.md risks. Clean-tree re-verification prevents Reviewer from trusting a producer's self-report, borrowed from Albert's verifier design.

items.title: Graph wiring — StateGraph, edges, interrupt points
items.description: Wire Architect, Driver (RED/GREEN modes), Reviewer, and Refactorer into a LangGraph StateGraph with the correct edges and interrupt pause points, per the RED -> Reviewer -> GREEN -> Reviewer -> Refactorer -> Reviewer loop (revised during architecture pass -- see ADR-0006 through ADR-0009 in docs/adrs/).
acceptance_criteria: A ticket flows Architect -> Driver -> Reviewer end-to-end with no interrupt trigger firing
Graph pauses at each defined interrupt point rather than proceeding silently
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 7
items.notes: Dependencies expanded during architecture pass before this ticket was started -- was originally BTN-4/5/6 only. Status reconciled 2026-08-02: graph.py implements full StateGraph wiring with battalion/graph.py test_graph.py passing; backlog.json had not been updated to reflect this.

items.title: Interrupt triggers (1-6) + budget tracking
items.description: Implement all 6 v1 interrupt triggers from spec.md, plus per-graph-run budget tracking (trigger #3).
acceptance_criteria: Each of the 6 triggers can be independently demonstrated with a reliable reproduction scenario
Trigger #1 increments only on same-root-cause rejections, not any rejection
Trigger #3 tracks budget per graph run, not per node
Trigger #5 (infra failure) has a distinct handling path, not folded into #1 or #3
Trigger #6 (manual checkpoint) pauses unconditionally at a user-declared phase, independent of any other trigger
items.source: spec.md Interrupt Taxonomy; plan.md sequencing step 8
items.notes: Critical/security-finding trigger intentionally excluded from v1 per spec.md. Trigger #1 now uses per-checkpoint-type counters (ADR-009, built in BTN-12), not a single ticket-wide counter. Status reconciled 2026-08-02: interrupts/triggers.py and interrupts/budget.py implement all 6 triggers with test_interrupts.py passing; backlog.json had not been updated to reflect this.

items.title: CLI (Typer) — run / resume / status
items.description: Typer-based CLI entry point wrapping the graph: run a new ticket, resume a paused run, check status.
acceptance_criteria: `battalion run` starts a new ticket through the graph
`battalion resume` continues a paused/interrupted run from saved state
`battalion status` reports current phase and any pending interrupt for a run
items.source: plan.md sequencing step 9, ADR-003
items.notes: Thinnest layer, wraps already-working internals — deliberately sequenced last among build tickets. Status updated 2026-08-02: cli.py implements all three commands with Typer, config via battalion.config.yaml, JSON/human output for status.

items.title: End-to-end acceptance criteria validation
items.description: Validate the full v1 milestone acceptance criteria from spec.md against the built system.
acceptance_criteria: All spec.md v1 acceptance criteria pass
A second CLI invocation resumes correctly from a prior run's state file
items.source: spec.md Acceptance Criteria; plan.md sequencing step 10
items.notes: This is the milestone gate for v1 completion. Status reconciled 2026-08-07: tests/test_acceptance.py validates all five spec.md v1 acceptance criteria plus BTN-10's own ACs against the built system, with real graph routing, real node implementations, real write-scope enforcement, and real clean-tree subprocess test execution (only LLM calls are faked). Validation surfaced and fixed four real defects that kept the milestone gate red: (1) Reviewer's clean-tree re-run used bare 'python' from PATH, which has no pytest outside the activated venv -- now uses sys.executable; (2) graph.py did not catch InfraFailure/ScopeViolationError from nodes, so triggers #2/#5 crashed invoke() with an unhandled exception instead of pausing -- node calls are now wrapped and routed to an AWAITING_HUMAN pause with the interrupt logged; (3) cli.py run/resume passed the graph's raw dict output to save_state, which requires RunState -- now validates via RunState.model_validate; (4) stale test_cli.py mocks predated run_ticket's spec_text kwarg -- updated. Full suite: 210 tests passing.

items.title: Driver RED/GREEN mode support
items.description: Add a mode: Literal['red','green'] parameter to run_driver (ADR-006). RED mode's prompt asks only for failing test files; GREEN mode's asks only for implementation files against tests that already exist. Both still produce the same {files: {...}} shape.
acceptance_criteria: run_driver accepts a mode parameter; omitting it preserves BTN-5's original combined behavior (non-breaking)
RED mode's system prompt instructs test-only output; GREEN mode's instructs implementation-only output against existing tests
Existing BTN-5 tests continue to pass unmodified
items.source: docs/adrs/adr0006.md
items.notes: Discovered during architecture pass before BTN-7, not part of original BTN-5 scope.

items.title: Reviewer expect_pass parameter + per-checkpoint rejection counters
items.description: Add expect_pass: bool to run_reviewer (ADR-007): accept means the test outcome matches expect_pass, not just 'tests passed'. Add a checkpoint field to RejectionRecord and compute cycle_number per-checkpoint-type rather than globally (ADR-009) -- state schema change, bump schema_version.
acceptance_criteria: expect_pass=False (RED-checkpoint) accepts when tests fail, rejects when they unexpectedly pass
expect_pass=True (GREEN/REFACTOR-checkpoint) behaves as BTN-6's original pass=accept logic
RejectionRecord.checkpoint field added; cycle_number increments independently per checkpoint type, confirmed by a test with rejections across two different checkpoints not sharing a counter
schema_version bumped; existing BTN-1 state persistence tests still pass
items.source: docs/adrs/adr0007.md; docs/adrs/adr0009.md
items.notes: The expect_pass gap was caught during the architecture pass, not discovered later during BTN-7 wiring -- flagged before any graph code depended on the old always-pass-is-accept behavior.

items.title: Refactorer node
items.description: New node, same shape as Driver: builds its own scoped write tools internally (ADR-008), but calls build_write_tools with node_name='driver' (not 'refactorer') since it shares Driver's declared src/ write_scope entry rather than getting its own. Refactors passing code without changing behavior; re-checked by Reviewer with expect_pass=True.
acceptance_criteria: run_refactorer produces file writes under src/, using Driver's write_scope entry (verified: no 'refactorer' key needed in write_scope for this to work)
Cannot write outside the shared scope (same structural guarantee as Driver, verified via BTN-2's test pattern)
Loads its own prompt from prompts/refactorer.md by default, with override support matching the other nodes
items.source: docs/adrs/adr0008.md
items.notes: New node discovered during architecture pass -- not in original v1 scope (Architect/Driver/Reviewer only). Status reconciled 2026-08-02: nodes/refactorer.py implements this per ADR-008 with test_refactorer_node.py passing; backlog.json had not been updated to reflect this.

items.title: Model-diversity constraint: Reviewer must differ from Driver
items.description: Structurally enforce that Reviewer's configured model differs from Driver's, so code isn't written and reviewed by the same model under different node labels. NodeLLMConfig/build_node_configs (BTN-3) already support per-node models -- this is a missing constraint, not new plumbing. Implemented in build_node_configs() and load_config() to raise ModelDiversityError when both driver and reviewer are explicitly configured with the same model.
acceptance_criteria: Configuring reviewer and driver with the same model raises a clear error before the graph can run
Configuring them with different models works unchanged
Error message names both node names and the shared model, not a generic validation failure
items.source: flagged in conversation after BTN-11 -- deliberately deferred, not in scope for BTN-12
items.notes: Implemented with ModelDiversityError in litellm_client.py and config.py. Only enforces when both driver and reviewer are explicitly configured (not just using defaults). Tests in test_model_diversity.py.

items.title: CLI setup command for LLM configuration and validation
items.description: Add a 'battalion setup' CLI command that interactively or declaratively configures LLM providers, API keys, and model selections, then validates connectivity to each configured model before saving to battalion.config.yaml. Reduces onboarding friction by handling provider prefixes, key validation, and model diversity constraints automatically.
acceptance_criteria: Running 'battalion setup' without a config file creates a valid battalion.config.yaml with working model configs
The setup command validates API key connectivity for each configured provider before completing
The setup command enforces model diversity between Driver and Reviewer automatically
Existing config files are preserved with only specified changes, not overwritten entirely
items.source: user request after trying initial CLI usage
items.notes: Motivated by the friction of manual config setup, provider prefix requirements, and API key management. Should integrate with LiteLLM's existing provider detection.

items.title: Cost/budget reporting granularity
items.description: Extend BTN-8's budget tracking with a per-node, per-call cost reporting layer: model, token counts in/out, and $ cost logged per call, plus a queryable summary broken down by node/phase for a given run. Additive on top of BTN-8's threshold-tracking behavior for trigger #3 -- does not change trigger #3's logic.
acceptance_criteria: Per-node, per-call cost is logged (model, input/output token counts, dollar cost), not just an aggregate running total
A summary view (e.g. `battalion status --costs` or equivalent) breaks down spend by node/phase for a given run
BTN-8's trigger #3 threshold behavior is unchanged by this ticket
Existing BTN-8 interrupt tests continue to pass unmodified
items.source: spun out of 2026-08-04 discussion re: portfolio-project overlap with Battalion's existing budget tracking
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. Each successful LiteLLM completion now records its call identifier, provider-reported model, input/output token counts, and US-dollar cost on the originating BTN-19 node execution. The execution-record contract is version 1.1 while persisted 1.0 records remain readable. `battalion status RUN_ID --costs` provides deterministic per-phase and run totals in JSON or human-readable form. ADR-0017 documents that cost observations are durable evidence and remain separate from BTN-8's unchanged integer turn budget and trigger #3 behavior. Full suite: 316 passed.

items.title: Interrupt/checkpoint web UI
items.description: Web UI surfacing interrupt_log and current status/phase for a run, so a human can see why the graph paused and approve/resume without the CLI. Wired to the existing CLI resume path, not a parallel code path. Explicitly scoped to interrupt visibility and resume/approve actions -- not a token-streaming chat interface.
acceptance_criteria: Displays interrupt_log and current status/phase for a given run
All 6 trigger types are surfaced distinctly, including trigger #1's per-checkpoint-type counters from BTN-12 (not flattened into a generic 'rejected' state)
Resume/approve action in the UI calls the same code path as `battalion resume`, not a duplicate implementation
No token-by-token streaming or chat-style interaction in scope for this ticket
items.source: spun out of 2026-08-04 discussion re: portfolio-project overlap; Luke's existing future-UI intent
items.notes: Cancelled as no longer required on 2026-08-13. Battalion's planned UI has diverged from this narrow interrupt/checkpoint surface, so implementing these acceptance criteria would create the wrong product boundary. No BTN-17 implementation was shipped. Future UI work must be specified and ticketed from the revised UI direction rather than treating this ticket as completed or silently reusing its scope.

items.title: Public GitHub Pages site
items.description: Publish README/architecture docs (spec.md, plan.md, ADRs) as a GitHub Pages site once v1 acceptance criteria pass. Scoped to Battalion only.
acceptance_criteria: GitHub Pages site publishes README, spec.md, plan.md, and ADR content from the Battalion repo
Site build requires BTN-10 to be done -- v1 is not advertised as working until its own acceptance criteria have passed
No Dojo or Writer's Bloc content included -- neither repo exists yet
items.source: spun out of 2026-08-04 discussion re: portfolio-site framing
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-11. The public site is deployed at https://lrburkholder.github.io/battalion/ via a GitHub Actions Pages workflow. Its explicit allowlist publishes README.md, spec.md, plan.md, LICENSE, and ADR-0001 through ADR-0012; draft Recon, Intel, and UI content is excluded. Live verification confirmed the landing page, spec, plan, and ADR index return HTTP 200, all checked internal links resolve, and the excluded documentation paths return HTTP 404. BTN-10 was already done before deployment. A future follow-up may expand the site to Dojo and Writer's Bloc if those repositories are created; they were deliberately not included in BTN-18.

items.title: Durable execution record and artifact provenance
items.description: Persist a durable, versioned record of each node execution so completed runs can be inspected by humans, Recon, and future observability surfaces without depending on transient conversation or logs.
acceptance_criteria: Each node execution records its role, phase, model identity, bounded input references, output or verdict, start/end timestamps, and outcome
Review results, test outcomes, tool activity, interrupts, and produced artifacts are linked to the node execution that created them
Artifact provenance identifies the originating run and node without embedding unbounded artifact contents in RunState
Execution records survive save, load, pause, resume, and completion
The persisted format is versioned and validated, with graph-level tests covering a complete run
items.source: docs/recon/backlogproposal.md; docs/intel/spec.md; docs/ui/spec.md; 2026-08-11 backlog reconciliation
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. RunState now contains a separately versioned execution record with one durable entry per Architect, Driver, Reviewer, and Refactorer attempt. Entries record bounded input references, model identity, timestamps, outcome, outputs or verdicts, test/review evidence, scoped-write activity, interrupts, and content-free artifact provenance (path plus SHA-256 and originating run/node IDs). Persistence, complete-run graph coverage, and pause/save/load/resume survival are tested. ADR-0014 and spec.md document the contract. Cost reporting, a web UI, and knowledge generation remain out of scope. Full suite: 277 passed.

items.title: Instinct data contract
items.description: Define the versioned contract for candidate and accepted Instincts, including recommendation, evidence, audience, applicability, tags, provenance, lifecycle status, and supersession metadata.
acceptance_criteria: The contract validates stable identifier, schema version, lifecycle status, recommendation, evidence references, audience, applicability, tags, and creation provenance
Candidate and accepted lifecycle states are explicit and validation prevents a candidate from masquerading as accepted knowledge
Supersession references another stable Instinct identifier while preserving the earlier record
Accepted Instincts contain enough evidence and scope to remain understandable without conversational context
Confidence is not assigned at creation; operational confidence remains deferred until feedback evidence exists
items.source: docs/recon/spec.md; docs/intel/spec.md; docs/adrs/adr0010.md; docs/adrs/adr0011.md; docs/adrs/adr0012.md
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. Added a strict, separately versioned Instinct contract with discriminated candidate and accepted types, bounded execution evidence, role audience, explicit applicability, tags, creation and human-acceptance provenance, and forward-only supersession references. Creation-time confidence is rejected and remains deferred pending operational feedback. Updated spec.md and the Intel/Recon drafts without presenting proposed ADR-0011 or ADR-0012 as shipped lifecycle behavior. Full suite: 291 passed.

items.title: Immutable Intel repository
items.description: Persist human-accepted Instincts under stable identifiers, enforce immutability, and preserve history when newer guidance supersedes older knowledge.
acceptance_criteria: Only accepted Instincts can be stored in the active Intel repository
An accepted Instinct cannot be edited or overwritten in place
Changed guidance is stored as a new Instinct that may supersede an earlier stable identifier
Superseded records remain retrievable for provenance but are excluded from active retrieval
Repository persistence and validation are covered without network services or embedding dependencies
items.source: docs/intel/spec.md; docs/adrs/adr0010.md; docs/adrs/adr0011.md
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. Added a local directory-backed Intel repository that stores only validated AcceptedInstinct records under stable identifiers using create-only writes. Existing records cannot be overwritten; replacements receive new identifiers and must reference an existing superseded record. Historical records remain directly retrievable while active listing excludes superseded guidance. Persistence, boundary validation, referential integrity, and tamper detection are covered without network or embedding dependencies. Full suite: 298 passed.

items.title: Recon candidate generation
items.description: Introduce Recon as a post-completion role that reads a durable execution record and produces zero or more evidence-backed candidate Instincts for human review.
acceptance_criteria: Recon runs only after a completed execution and receives the BTN-19 execution record rather than transient conversation state
Recon emits zero or more candidate Instincts that validate against BTN-20
Every candidate cites evidence from the completed execution and scopes where its recommendation applies
Recon avoids proposing a candidate that duplicates an existing accepted Instinct supplied for comparison
Recon cannot publish knowledge, modify standards or architecture, affect the completed run, or bypass human review
items.source: docs/recon/spec.md; docs/recon/backlogproposal.md; docs/adrs/adr0011.md
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. Added Recon as a post-completion, read-only role that consumes the BTN-19 durable execution record and accepted Instincts supplied for duplicate comparison. Candidate output is validated against BTN-20, mechanically tied to real execution evidence, de-duplicated, and returned separately from RunState. Recon has no write or Intel repository authority. ADR-0015 and spec.md record the boundary and correct the older draft's transient conversation-history input. Full suite: 306 passed.

items.title: Operator review and Instinct promotion workflow
items.description: Provide an explicit human workflow to accept, edit then accept, or reject each Recon candidate, with only approved knowledge promoted into the Intel repository.
acceptance_criteria: The operator can accept, edit then accept, or reject each candidate independently
Accepting validates the candidate and stores a new immutable accepted Instinct through BTN-21
Editing creates the accepted content without mutating the original Recon candidate or its provenance
Rejected candidates never become eligible for retrieval
Every decision records the operator action, timestamp, candidate identifier, and resulting accepted identifier when applicable
items.source: docs/recon/spec.md; docs/intel/spec.md; docs/adrs/adr0011.md; philosophy.md

items.title: Deterministic retrieval and node-specific Instinct injection
items.description: Retrieve accepted, active Instincts with explicit rules and assemble bounded, role-specific knowledge context through Battalion's canonical context path.
acceptance_criteria: Retrieval considers only accepted, active, non-superseded Instincts
Selection uses deterministic audience, tag, and applicability rules with stable ordering and documented tie-breaking
Each execution role receives only Instincts relevant to that role and task
Injected context is bounded, identifies every supplied Instinct, and is assembled through BTN-26 rather than a parallel prompt path
Tests demonstrate distinct role-specific selections and explain why included and excluded Instincts were selected
Semantic or embedding-based retrieval, operational feedback, confidence scoring, and cross-project sharing remain out of scope
items.source: docs/intel/spec.md; docs/adrs/adr0011.md; 2026-08-11 backlog reconciliation
items.notes: This is the smallest inspectable retrieval vertical slice. Confidence ranking must wait until real operator-feedback evidence exists; ADR-0012 remains future-facing.

items.title: Align role prompts with node contracts
items.description: Tighten Architect, Driver, Reviewer, and Refactorer prompts around their actual authority, inputs, output parsers, write-root semantics, and checkpoint responsibilities.
acceptance_criteria: Every file-producing prompt requires the exact files JSON contract and paths relative to the bound src root
RED, GREEN, Reviewer, and Refactorer prompts do not claim authority or execution capabilities their nodes do not have
Reviewer emits only a normalized rejection-cause sentence compatible with same-cause detection
Architect distinguishes evidence, assumptions, decisions, open questions, and deferred work
Static prompt-contract tests protect the mechanically significant instructions
items.source: 2026-08-11 prompt review
items.notes: Prompt-only improvement. Context propagation is tracked separately in BTN-26.

items.title: Persist and assemble node execution context
items.description: Preserve the supplied specification in RunState and assemble bounded, role-appropriate context for Architect, Driver RED/GREEN, and Refactorer instead of passing only ticket_id.
acceptance_criteria: RunState persists the supplied specification across save, load, pause, and resume
Architect receives the specification rather than only the ticket ID
Driver receives the specification, approved plan, and relevant existing test or implementation context for its mode
Refactorer receives the passing files it is expected to improve
Context assembly is deterministic, bounded, and covered by graph-level tests
items.source: discovered during 2026-08-11 prompt review
items.notes: Implemented with a backward-compatible RunState spec field and one deterministic, bounded context assembler used by Architect, Driver RED/GREEN, and Refactorer.

items.title: Preserve caller-supplied run configuration
items.description: Make the CLI and reusable runtime execute the same caller-supplied RunState contract instead of constructing configuration-aware state in the CLI and then replacing it with hardcoded defaults inside run_ticket.
acceptance_criteria: The CLI passes one caller-created initial RunState into the reusable graph execution path rather than allowing run_ticket to recreate it
Configured budget limit, manual checkpoints, write scope, specification, retry bound, run identifier, and ticket identifier are preserved through initial invocation
Pause and resume preserve the same run configuration without resetting fields to runtime defaults
The reusable run API has one documented source of truth for initial state and rejects conflicting duplicate configuration
A CLI-level acceptance test proves that non-default budget, checkpoint, and write-scope values reach graph execution unchanged
Existing run, resume, persistence, interrupt, and BTN-10 acceptance behavior remains passing
items.source: 2026-08-11 backlog reconciliation; battalion/cli.py run command; battalion/graph.py run_ticket
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. The CLI now passes its complete caller-created RunState to run_ticket, whose signature makes that state the sole source of initial run configuration and rejects duplicate ticket/specification configuration. Regression coverage proves non-default identifiers, specification, budget, checkpoints, write scope, and retry bound reach initial graph invocation unchanged; resume preserves the saved configuration. Reusable API behavior is documented in README.md. Focused graph/CLI/acceptance tests: 55 passed. Full suite: 261 passed.

items.title: Project-layout-aware scoped writes
items.description: Generalize Driver RED/GREEN and Refactorer write roots so Battalion can operate on explicitly declared project layouts instead of requiring every project to place both tests and implementation under a hardcoded src/ directory.
acceptance_criteria: Run configuration can declare distinct allowed test and implementation roots for Driver RED, Driver GREEN, and Refactorer without weakening per-node structural scope enforcement
RED output is restricted to declared test roots and test-file shapes; GREEN and Refactorer output are restricted to declared implementation roots
Reviewer verification runs against the configured project root and does not assume tests live under src/
Battalion's own root-level battalion/ and tests/ layout can be represented without granting a writing node repository-wide authority
Traversal, absolute-path, undeclared-root, and cross-role write attempts remain mechanically blocked and independently tested
Default configuration preserves existing src/-layout behavior for current users
The write-scope contract, role authority impact, and migration behavior are recorded in the relevant specification and an accepted ADR
items.source: 2026-08-11 dogfooding reconciliation; docs/adrs/adr0002.md; battalion/scope/tool_binding.py; battalion/nodes/driver.py
items.notes: Completed 2026-08-13. ADR-0013 adds explicit driver_red, driver_green, and refactorer phase scopes with legacy driver fallback, preserving the default src/ layout. Each phase builds only its selected bound tools; multi-root output requires a declared root prefix and batches are fully validated before writes. Reviewer now verifies a clean copy of the configured project root while excluding local runtime metadata. Battalion's tests/ plus battalion/ layout is covered without repository-wide write authority, and context/prompt contracts follow the configured roots. Focused scope/node suite: 86 passed. Reviewer suite: 29 passed. Prompt/graph contracts: 37 passed. Full suite: 273 passed.

items.title: Desktop operator interface architecture RFC
items.description: Define Battalion's desktop-first operator experience and the application boundaries needed to execute, inspect, search, and intervene in human-directed runs without coupling the product to an IDE, a hosted observability service, or a parallel graph-control path.
acceptance_criteria: RFC-0004 defines the product information hierarchy for projects, tickets, runs, node executions, artifacts, interrupts, operator decisions, and Instincts using the implemented Battalion contracts

The primary desktop workflows cover starting and observing work, inspecting execution evidence and provenance, safely intervening, resolving interrupts, reviewing Recon candidates, and navigating history

The design identifies which views can be derived from RunState, ExecutionRecord, cost observations, Intel repositories, and operator decision records, and explicitly identifies evidence the current contracts do not yet capture
CLI and graphical clients share reusable application commands for run, resume, inspection, and human-authorized actions; the UI does not invoke LangGraph or mutate persisted state directly

The RFC defines functionally equivalent, disposable Tauri, PySide6, and Electron follow-up spikes that exercise the same bounded fake-data workflow and record comparable packaging, process, resource, accessibility, testability, failure-recovery, permission-surface, learning, and implementation-complexity evidence before framework selection

The RFC decomposes expected follow-up work including the shared application boundary, run identity, operator summaries, Recon candidate persistence, usage semantics, live observation, a common benchmark fixture, three framework spikes, the framework-selection ADR, and production UI vertical slices without reserving ticket identifiers prematurely

Search, model-effectiveness analytics, optional mobile history access, privacy and retention, crash recovery, and future persistence/indexing needs are scoped with explicit decisions or open questions rather than presented as shipped behavior
The older draft UI documents and cancelled BTN-17 web UI scope are reconciled so they cannot be mistaken for the current interface contract
No production UI implementation, framework spike implementation, mobile execution control, semantic index, model router, or replacement persistence authority is introduced by this ticket
items.source: 2026-08-11 through 2026-08-13 UI design discussion; docs/ui/; ADR-0014; ADR-0016; ADR-0017; ADR-0018
items.notes: Accepted by the human operator on 2026-08-14. RFC-0004 establishes the desktop-first product direction, shared application boundary, one-worker-per-active-run model, UUID run identity direction, bounded revision and prompt provenance, persisted Markdown Recon candidates, typed next-attempt interventions, cost semantics, and equivalent Tauri/PySide6/Electron follow-up spikes. The six remaining open questions are intentionally deferred to implementation and operational evidence. No production UI or framework spike was implemented by BTN-29.

items.title: Application command and query boundary
items.description: Extract a reusable Python application boundary for run, resume, inspection, and human-authorized operations so the CLI and future graphical clients share policy and persistence behavior.
acceptance_criteria: Reusable application commands and queries cover the first desktop vertical slice without importing a UI or transport framework
The CLI delegates applicable run, resume, inspection, and human-authorized operations to the shared boundary instead of maintaining a parallel implementation
Application operations return typed results and documented domain failures suitable for both CLI rendering and graphical clients
The boundary preserves RunState, graph, interrupt, write-scope, and persistence authority rather than allowing clients to mutate state directly
Focused tests prove equivalent behavior through the shared boundary and existing CLI entry points
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Application command and query boundary
items.notes: The precise smallest command/query surface is intentionally expected to emerge from the first vertical slice. Keep it framework- and transport-neutral.

items.title: Active-run worker supervision
items.description: Supervise one isolated Python worker process per active run, with explicit lifecycle, failure, reconnect, and recovery behavior for desktop clients.
acceptance_criteria: Each active run executes in its own supervised Python process and has a stable association with its canonical run identity
Starting, observing, cancelling, and reconnecting to workers occur through the application boundary
Worker crashes and client disconnections preserve the durable execution record and surface an explicit recoverable or terminal state
A desktop-client crash does not silently terminate or corrupt unrelated active runs
Tests cover concurrent workers, abnormal termination, restart or reconnect behavior, and cleanup without making provider calls
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Active-run worker supervision
items.notes: Implemented on 2026-08-14. ADR-0019 records detached one-process-per-run supervision, project-local lifecycle records, application-boundary start/observe/cancel/reconnect operations, atomic RunState persistence, and per-node durable checkpoints. Focused tests cover concurrent associations, duplicate launch prevention, abnormal exit recovery, reconnect, cancellation isolation, detached client lifetime, entrypoint completion, and malformed metadata without provider calls; the full suite passes.

items.title: Run and project identity
items.description: Introduce generated UUID run identifiers, separate display aliases, and durable project identity semantics that tolerate repository moves and existing human-readable run IDs.
acceptance_criteria: New runs receive collision-resistant UUID canonical identifiers independently of their human-readable display aliases
Persisted references use canonical identifiers while user-facing views can retain meaningful ticket and run labels
A documented migration or compatibility path preserves access to existing runs with human-readable identifiers
Project identity and catalog behavior recognize or explicitly reconcile a repository that moves on disk without silently merging distinct projects
Tests cover duplicate display aliases, moved repositories, legacy records, malformed identities, and cross-project isolation
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Run and project identity
items.notes: Implemented 2026-08-16. ADR-0020 records UUIDv4 canonical run IDs, separate display aliases, project-local UUID markers and rebuildable run catalogs, duplicate-copy reconciliation, and a non-destructive legacy compatibility projection. New identity creation is owned by the shared application boundary; graph execution cannot replace canonical identity. Focused tests cover duplicate aliases, moved repositories and catalogs, duplicate live copies, legacy records, malformed project markers and references, and cross-project isolation. Full suite: 346 tests passing.

items.title: Operator summaries and revision evidence
items.description: Persist bounded handoff-style operator summaries and enough model, prompt, revision, context, artifact, and verification metadata to inspect what happened without retaining source code or prompt contents by default.
acceptance_criteria: Each relevant node attempt can record what it did, what should happen next, open questions, and the last role or node that worked
Evidence records model and configuration identity, role, phase, prompt contract version, prompt template hash and algorithm, and Battalion revision
Code provenance records base commit object ID and algorithm, branch or detached state, start and end dirty state, bounded input hashes, and output artifact hashes
Context provenance records bounded references, hashes, inclusion reasons, and truncation metadata without retaining source code, prompt templates, or rendered prompts by default
The record clearly labels when a dirty workspace cannot be reconstructed exactly because no patch content was retained
Schema validation, compatibility behavior, and serialization round trips are covered by tests
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Operator-summary and revision evidence
items.notes: Implemented 2026-08-16. Execution record schema 1.2 adds bounded operator handoffs; prompt contract, template hash, model-configuration identity, and Battalion revision evidence; Git base/branch/dirty-state provenance; and bounded context hashes with inclusion and truncation metadata. Dirty workspaces explicitly record that exact reconstruction is unavailable because patches are not retained. Legacy 1.0 and 1.1 records remain readable, configuration values and prompt/source contents are not persisted, and save/load round trips preserve the evidence. Focused refactored unit/integration slice: 26 tests passing. Full suite: 351 tests passing.

items.title: Recon candidate persistence
items.description: Persist Recon output as immutable, create-only Markdown candidates with validated metadata and deterministic inbox discovery before human review and Instinct promotion.
acceptance_criteria: Recon candidates are persisted as human-readable Markdown with a strict validated metadata contract
Candidate creation is create-only and collision-safe; existing candidate contents cannot be overwritten through the persistence API
The review inbox discovers candidates deterministically and distinguishes pending, promoted, and rejected disposition without mutating candidate evidence
Malformed metadata, path traversal, duplicate creation, and partial-write behavior fail safely and are tested
Creation-time confidence is not introduced, preserving ADR-0012 and BTN-20 semantics
The repository path and rejected-candidate retention policy are documented from implementation and usage evidence
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Recon candidate persistence
items.notes: Implemented 2026-08-17 on the BTN-34 branch. Recon candidates use strict YAML front matter plus deterministic human-readable Markdown under .battalion/recon/candidates. Atomic create-only publication prevents overwrite and partial destination files; the deterministic inbox projects pending, promoted, or rejected from separate immutable decisions without mutating candidate evidence. Rejected candidates are retained indefinitely and no deletion API is exposed. Focused Intel/Recon/docs slice: 46 tests passing. Full suite: 352 tests passing.

items.title: Usage evidence revision
items.description: Revise usage evidence to represent provider-reported or calculated cost with nullable decimal amount, currency, source, and explicit unknown semantics.
acceptance_criteria: Usage evidence stores cost as a nullable decimal amount rather than binary floating point
Cost currency and cost source are stored separately and validated when a cost amount is present
Unknown, unavailable, provider-reported, and locally calculated cost states remain distinguishable
Existing token usage remains inspectable when monetary cost is unknown
Serialization, aggregation, compatibility, and malformed-value behavior are covered by tests
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Usage evidence revision
items.notes: Implemented 2026-08-17. Execution-record schema 1.2 stores nullable Decimal cost with separately validated ISO 4217 currency and provider-reported, estimated, or unknown source. Missing cost remains null while tokens remain inspectable; legacy 1.1 cost_usd evidence loads as provider-reported USD without rewriting history. Currency-aware projections preserve exact decimal strings and count unknown-cost calls. Full suite: 349 tests passing.

items.title: Live observation contract
items.description: Define and implement the framework-neutral observation contract for active runs, including durable and transient event categories and reload-after-disconnect behavior.
acceptance_criteria: The contract distinguishes durable evidence that can be reconstructed after reload from transient progress signals that may be lost
Events have stable run, node or attempt, ordering, and timestamp semantics sufficient for multiple concurrent active runs
A reconnecting client rebuilds authoritative state from persistence before consuming newer live events
The observation path cannot mutate graph state or bypass canonical interrupt and resume operations
Tests cover ordering, duplicate delivery, missed transient events, disconnect and reconnect, and malformed event handling
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Live observation contract
items.notes: Implemented 2026-08-17. ADR-0021 records immutable versioned events ordered per canonical run and operation stream, with stable event IDs, timezone-aware timestamps, node-attempt identity, explicit durable, transient, and action-required categories, idempotent duplicate delivery, and malformed-event validation. Application callbacks publish typed observations only after durable checkpoints are saved. Reconnect captures a live barrier, reloads authoritative RunState through inspection, then permits post-barrier consumption; bounded transports may lose transient progress without becoming a state authority. Full suite: 354 tests passing.

items.title: Desktop framework benchmark fixture
items.description: Build the shared fake project, run history, simulated transitions, operator actions, and measurement procedure used unchanged by all three desktop framework spikes.
acceptance_criteria: The fixture provides deterministic fake projects, tickets, runs, node attempts, artifacts, interrupts, Recon candidates, usage, and provenance evidence
The scenario exercises Work, History, execution inspection, cost and provenance display, live transitions, reconnect, interrupt resolution, candidate review, Correction, and Design decision actions
No fixture path invokes a real model provider or depends on developer credentials
The measurement procedure defines comparable packaging, process, resource, accessibility, testability, failure-recovery, permission-surface, learning, and implementation-complexity observations
Tauri, PySide6, and Electron spikes can consume the same scenario and acceptance script without framework-specific changes
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Framework benchmark fixture
items.notes: Implemented 2026-08-17. benchmarks/desktop exports deterministic framework-neutral JSON for two fake projects, tickets, completed and interrupted runs, node attempts, artifacts, sourced and unknown usage, bounded provenance, Recon candidates, typed live transitions, and simulated operator actions. One ordered scenario and acceptance validator are shared unchanged by Tauri, PySide6, and Electron. The measurement template covers packaging, process, resources, accessibility, testability, failure recovery, permissions, learning, and implementation complexity. Fixture code imports no provider boundary, reads no credentials, and tests verify secret-independent deterministic output. Focused BTN-37 and Pages slice: 11 tests passing. Full suite: 373 tests passing.

items.title: Tauri desktop architecture spike
items.description: Implement the common desktop benchmark fixture as a disposable Tauri prototype and record the evidence needed for framework selection.
acceptance_criteria: The prototype completes the shared benchmark scenario without changing its application contract or measurement procedure
Packaging, startup, idle and active resource use, accessibility, automated testing, worker failure and reconnect behavior, and permission surface are measured
The implementation records Rust and Tauri learning demands, boundary complexity, platform constraints, and significant framework-specific code
The spike is clearly isolated from production code and can be discarded after the framework decision
Findings use the common evidence template and include reproducible build and benchmark instructions
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Tauri architecture spike
items.notes: Rust unfamiliarity is learning evidence, not an automatic negative; the spike should measure whether the resulting boundary and product are worth that investment.

items.title: PySide6 desktop architecture spike
items.description: Implement the common desktop benchmark fixture as a disposable PySide6 prototype and record the evidence needed for framework selection.
acceptance_criteria: The prototype completes the shared benchmark scenario without changing its application contract or measurement procedure
Packaging, startup, idle and active resource use, accessibility, automated testing, worker failure and reconnect behavior, and permission surface are measured
The implementation records Python and Qt learning demands, boundary complexity, platform constraints, and significant framework-specific code
The spike is clearly isolated from production code and can be discarded after the framework decision
Findings use the common evidence template and include reproducible build and benchmark instructions
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: PySide6 architecture spike
items.notes: The spike must exercise the same workflow as Tauri and Electron rather than optimizing for Python-specific convenience.

items.title: Electron desktop architecture spike
items.description: Implement the common desktop benchmark fixture as a disposable Electron prototype and record the evidence needed for framework selection.
acceptance_criteria: The prototype completes the shared benchmark scenario without changing its application contract or measurement procedure
Packaging, startup, idle and active resource use, accessibility, automated testing, worker failure and reconnect behavior, and permission surface are measured
The implementation records TypeScript and Electron learning demands, boundary complexity, platform constraints, and significant framework-specific code
The spike is clearly isolated from production code and can be discarded after the framework decision
Findings use the common evidence template and include reproducible build and benchmark instructions
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Electron architecture spike
items.notes: The spike must measure Electron as a desktop shell for Battalion, not assume web familiarity outweighs process, packaging, or resource evidence.

items.title: Desktop framework selection ADR
items.description: Compare the three framework spikes using their common evidence and record the selected production desktop framework in an accepted ADR.
acceptance_criteria: The ADR compares Tauri, PySide6, and Electron against every measurement category defined by the shared fixture
Claims are traceable to reproducible spike evidence and distinguish measurements from judgment
The decision considers human and machine learning, maintainability, application-boundary integrity, packaging, platform support, accessibility, testing, recovery, security, and resource cost
The ADR selects one production framework or explicitly records why more bounded evidence is required
Disposable spike code is not silently promoted into production without reconciliation against Battalion architecture and repository standards
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Desktop framework ADR
items.notes: Framework choice follows the three equivalent spikes; no candidate is preferred solely because of current language familiarity.

items.title: Read-only desktop operator console
items.description: Deliver the first production desktop vertical slice for browsing Work, History, execution evidence, provenance, token and cost usage, and the Intel library without state-changing controls.
acceptance_criteria: The selected desktop framework presents project and ticket Work views, run History, and detailed node-attempt inspection through the shared application boundary
Execution detail displays model, role, phase, prompt version and hash, Git revision and dirty-state limitations, bounded context provenance, artifacts, verification, tokens, and cost source semantics
The Intel library and persisted Recon candidates are discoverable without allowing the read-only slice to promote, reject, resume, or mutate them
Active runs update through the live observation contract and recover authoritative state after client restart or disconnect
Empty, loading, malformed, legacy, unknown-cost, crashed-worker, and inaccessible-project states are explicitly represented and tested
The UI never invokes LangGraph or edits persisted RunState directly
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Read-only operator console
items.notes: This is the first production UI slice after framework selection. It deliberately establishes trustworthy visibility before state-changing controls.

items.title: Desktop human-action surfaces
items.description: Add canonical interrupt resolution and Recon candidate review to the desktop client, followed by typed next-attempt Correction and Design decision context.
acceptance_criteria: Interrupt resolution and resume use the same application operations and graph-control path as the CLI
Recon candidates can be reviewed, promoted, or rejected through canonical Intel workflows without mutating immutable candidate evidence
Correction targets Driver RED, Driver GREEN, or Refactorer, while Design decision targets Architect
Interventions are queued as bounded context for the next attempt and do not steer an in-flight model generation
Reviewer-targeted intervention, Reviewer verdict override, and manual checkpoint override are not introduced
Every human action records actor, time, target, disposition, and resulting durable state and is covered by authorization and failure-path tests
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Human-action surfaces
items.notes: Any change to role authority, interrupt semantics, or graph transitions discovered here requires specification and ADR reconciliation before implementation.

items.title: History search and model-role analytics projections
items.description: Build rebuildable projections for run-history search and descriptive model-by-role evidence without turning correlation into automated model selection claims.
acceptance_criteria: Operators can search run history across tickets, summaries, roles, models, phases, outcomes, interrupts, verification, artifacts, and Intel references using rebuildable derived indexes
Search indexes can be deleted and reconstructed from canonical persisted evidence without data loss
Analytics compare model-role observations using transparent measures such as attempts, outcomes, review results, tokens, cost, duration, and available ticket characteristics
Unknown and incomparable evidence is displayed explicitly; small samples and confounding ticket characteristics are not presented as effectiveness conclusions
No automatic model router, hidden score, or replacement source of truth is introduced
Projection versioning, migration, filtering, and representative search and aggregation behavior are tested
items.source: RFC-0004 Expected Follow-Up Tickets: Search and analytics projections
items.notes: Objective ticket characteristics and any later semantic-search approach should emerge from accumulated usage evidence. This ticket begins with descriptive, rebuildable projections.

items.title: Specifier role architecture RFC
items.description: Decide whether Battalion should add a Specifier role and define the human-reviewed specification artifact, authority boundary, lifecycle, and graph relationship before any implementation.
acceptance_criteria: The RFC compares keeping specification authoring outside Battalion, running a separate pre-run workflow, and adding a graph phase without assuming that a new role is required
The proposed specification artifact, provenance, persistence owner, versioning, and relationship to canonical ticket identity are explicit
Human review, edit, acceptance, rejection, cancellation, ambiguity, and conflicting-source behavior are defined without allowing generated product decisions to become authoritative silently
Any proposed role has exact inputs, outputs, write scope, tools, prompt contract, model policy, context budget, execution evidence, cost semantics, and failure behavior
Graph placement, run identity, Architect handoff, checkpoints, interrupts, resume behavior, and application operations are reconciled with existing contracts
Representative workflow evidence and operator-correction measures support the decision, and accepted implementation work is split into separate tickets with required specification and ADR updates
items.source: README Future Architecture Planning; docs/future/specifier-role.md
items.notes: Planning only. The ticket may reject a Specifier role or keep it outside the execution graph; no role, prompt, state, or graph implementation is authorized.

items.title: Plugin architecture and integration lifecycle RFC
items.description: Specify permissioned extension points and a complete plugin lifecycle without weakening write scopes, application policy, secret handling, offline operation, or repository sources of truth.
acceptance_criteria: The RFC defines a minimal extension-point taxonomy and explicitly identifies graph, state, interrupt, scope, and human-decision boundaries that plugins cannot replace
Manifest identity, provenance, versioning, compatibility, dependencies, discovery, installation, enablement, configuration, update, disablement, removal, and retained-data behavior are specified
Filesystem, process, network, credential, model, ticket, and application-operation capabilities require explicit least-authority grants with inspectable defaults
Secret ownership, redaction, context exclusion, audit evidence, isolation, timeout, cancellation, crash recovery, and offline degradation semantics are defined
The threat model covers malicious, stale, compromised, over-privileged, incompatible, and unavailable plugins plus source-of-truth conflicts and duplicate remote mutation
A disposable integration scenario validates the proposed boundary, and accepted runtime, SDK, packaging, marketplace, and example integration work is split into separate tickets and ADRs
items.source: README Future Architecture Planning; docs/future/plugin-architecture.md
items.notes: Planning only. Live JIRA, MCP, repository, model-provider, or other integrations remain examples rather than accepted implementation scope.

items.title: Severity-based review and Guardian role RFC
items.description: Determine whether severity-based review belongs in existing Reviewer and interrupt policy or warrants a distinct Guardian role with a separate evidence and authority boundary.
acceptance_criteria: The RFC compares no new behavior, focused mechanical tooling, Reviewer policy specialization, and a distinct Guardian role without assuming that another graph node is beneficial
Objective trigger inputs, severity taxonomy, classification ownership, uncertainty, false positives, and human correction behavior are defined
Any proposed role has distinct responsibilities, inputs, outputs, prompt contract, model policy, write scope, durable evidence, and pass, finding, retry, failure, and cancellation semantics
Graph placement and every transition are reconciled with RED, GREEN, refactor, Reviewer, interrupt, manual-checkpoint, human-resolution, and resume contracts
Representative low- and high-impact cases compare finding quality, duplicate feedback, operator burden, explainability, latency, cost, and failure modes
The RFC records a no-role, policy-only, or bounded-role decision and splits accepted graph, state, prompt, interrupt, UI, test, specification, and ADR work into separate tickets
items.source: README Future Architecture Planning; docs/future/guardian-role.md
items.notes: Planning only. Model-assigned severity is not authoritative, and no Guardian node or new checkpoint is accepted by this ticket's creation.

items.title: Bounded self-modification safety and evidence RFC
items.description: Define whether and how Battalion may propose changes to its own graph and role definitions through isolated, reviewable, human-authorized engineering workflows without runtime self-editing or self-approval.
acceptance_criteria: The RFC defines self-modification as version-controlled change proposals and explicitly forbids same-run mutation, automatic approval, merge, deployment, permission expansion, or protection bypass

A threat model covers authority escalation, prompt or review tampering, compromised state, recursive execution, stale bases, malicious changes, validation evasion, secret exposure, and rollback failure
Human checkpoints for objective, architecture, scope, validation, acceptance, merge, rollout, rollback, and mechanical stop are explicit and cannot be satisfied solely by the proposing execution

Isolation between the running trusted Battalion instance and candidate worktree or environment is defined together with provenance for objectives, plans, prompts, models, tools, diffs, tests, reviews, decisions, and revisions

A staged evidence plan begins with read-only analysis and disposable patch proposals and includes rejection, failed validation, protected-surface edits, independent review, recovery, budget, recursion, and stop conditions
The RFC makes explicit go, no-go, and stop decisions for each stage, may reject the capability entirely, and requires separate human-approved tickets for every experiment or implementation
items.source: README Future Architecture Planning; docs/future/self-modification.md
items.notes: Long-term research planning only. Dogfooding does not authorize autonomous self-editing, and this ticket must not change runtime graph, role, scope, interrupt, merge, or deployment authority.
